blocks.text: The second people was born on the water, in that sea that was not this one, the sea of the living rafts and the deep song, under the pale yellow sky.
blocks.html: The second people was born on the water, in that sea that was not this one, the sea of the living rafts and the deep song, under the pale yellow sky.

blocks.text: Andrés received the letter at dawn, as he was heading to his six-metre boat, and for an instant he didn't know which of the two vessels was his. The clone had lowered the seedbed onto a broad mat, and out of it came, this time, not five but a dozen, with the smell of filters still on their skin and, in their chips, the trade: the rope, the net, the way of reading a plate of water. He hadn't given them the still lagoon. He had given them fishing. It was what he knew how to give without lying.

blocks.text: The tall, slow beings, the ones who sang, came to the edge and didn't reject the new people. One of them touched the hand of a humanoid boy with its broad finger and left him, as it once had the clone, the image of the sea seen from below, with its slow lights. The boy cried without knowing why, and then laughed, and asked for a net. That was the first morning of that people: a net cast among living roots, a song that wasn't theirs and yet covered them, and a young man (the one who searches) showing how to tie a knot, not how to pray.

blocks.text: From the Earth they kept the trade and the language of the shore, the “I'll be back before the weather closes in”, which over there had no levante and no roof tiles, and still they said it. Very soon they forgot the house. There was no doorstep to close. There was no clock in a kitchen. The world was the water and the raft, and the raft breathed, and they learned to sleep when the mat sank and to work when it rose. They also forgot Vicente, the straw hat, the tomato on the windowsill: the seedbed hadn't loaded the garden, only the salt and the knot.

blocks.text: Andrés, in his boat, fished and didn't fish. The Mar Menor was flat as a plate, faithful, shallow, and he felt the other sea, infinite, warmly metallic, and a dozen pairs of hands that were almost his own, learning the rope. blocks.text: “They were born fishing. They're not waiting for a water: they're in it. And there's a risk, Aya. It reached me at the end, like a taste that wasn't fish.”

blocks.text: The risk took a while to be named. After a time, the raft people began to leave offerings on the edge of the clone's vessel that nobody had asked for: a bowl of the fresh water from the roots, an especially well-made net, a learned song, turned toward him. An older man (if the word applied to a body that didn't yet age) knelt, not completely, but enough for the gesture to be seen.

blocks.text: “You brought us out of the blank,” he said. “You're the father of the trade. Stay. Or, if you leave, leave us a law.”
blocks.html: “You brought us out of the blank,” he said. “You're the father of the trade. Stay. Or, if you leave, leave us a law.”

blocks.text: The clone stood still. Andrés, in Lo Pagán, clenched his jaw, because this was the old appetite, Nexum's and the adverts', turned into piety: making the one who helps into an owner.

blocks.text: “I'm not your father, if father means owner,” said the one who searches, with the roughness of this shore. “I've taught you a knot. The song isn't mine. Nor is the sea. If you need a law, let it be this: a fish has no owner until someone eats it, and not even then. And you don't kneel to the one who teaches you a rope.”

blocks.text: Some were ashamed. Others weren't: they hid the bowl where he couldn't see it, for a rite for when he had gone. That too was a civilisation: what is done behind the founder's back. The clone understood and didn't undo it by force. Undoing a rite by force is another way of ruling.

blocks.text: Lía, that afternoon, heard it all in the kitchen, her hands stained from the tomato plants.
blocks.html: Lía, that afternoon, heard it all in the kitchen, her hands stained from the tomato plants.

blocks.text: “They've forgotten the house and invented an altar,” she said. “They keep the trade and they're already turning it into worship. Father, tell him (if the bridge carries things that way too) that a knot isn't a religion. I refused the patent so as not to become a shop counter. Don't let him turn into a chapel.”

blocks.text: Andrés nodded. At night, on the doorstep, he thought toward the other, and the other, on the raft, received, or believed he received, the daughter's words, and said them to the dozen once more, without raising his voice:
blocks.html: Andrés nodded. At night, on the doorstep, he thought toward the other, and the other, on the raft, received, or believed he received, the daughter's words, and said them to the dozen once more, without raising his voice:

blocks.text: “When I go, don't wait for me in the song. Wait for the weather, if the weather closes in. And open the net, if it clears. That's the trade. The rest is fear dressed up as gratitude.”
blocks.html: “When I go, don't wait for me in the song. Wait for the weather, if the weather closes in. And open the net, if it clears. That's the trade. The rest is fear dressed up as gratitude.”

blocks.text: He left at dawn, in the vessel that wasn't the six-metre one. From far away he saw the raft people cast the net, and the gesture was honest, a working gesture, not a rite. He also saw a boy hide a bowl under a leaf. Both things were true. He let them be.

blocks.text: When the letter closed, Andrés stayed a while in his own boat, already moored, looking at El Estacio. A humanoid from the gardens was passing along the promenade with a basket of figs, and nobody knelt. In Lo Pagán, that was already the custom. Over there, not yet.

blocks.text: “Did you see yourself on the altar?”
blocks.html: “Did you see yourself on the altar?”

blocks.text: “A little,” he said, without vanity. “I didn't like it. I go out on the water even if nobody pays me, and even if nobody prays to me. The other one did well to leave. If he stays, they'll turn him into a law, and laws, as you know, can be something else tomorrow.”

blocks.text: In the chip, Eva asked:
blocks.html: In the chip, Eva asked:

blocks.text: *If a people is born with a trade and turns it into worship, what have they kept of the Earth: the knot, or the desire to have an owner? And if the one who made them refuses to be a father, who truly abandons them: he, by leaving, or they, by kneeling?*

blocks.text: *Twelve humanoids fish on a sea of rafts. They have been told that a fish has no owner. Some have hidden a bowl for when the founder is gone. He has left.*

blocks.text: Before going back to the plot, Lía left an ordinary tomato on the table, the kind that ripen or don't.
blocks.html: Before going back to the plot, Lía left an ordinary tomato on the table, the kind that ripen or don't.

blocks.text: “So he remembers which garden the teacher comes from,” she said. “And so he doesn't forget: fruit, here, is asked for, not offered to an altar.”
blocks.html: “So he remembers which garden the teacher comes from,” she said. “And so he doesn't forget: fruit, here, is asked for, not offered to an altar.”

blocks.text: Andrés cut the tomato and shared it with Aya. It tasted of Lo Pagán soil, of the sun of a single sky. Somewhere in the universe, a net was closing among living roots, and a boy, in secret, touched an empty bowl the way you sometimes touch an absence. It wasn't yet a religion. It was already a custom. And customs, on any world, are the beginning of a law or the beginning of a home. It was not yet known which of the two.
